name: Gil Kalai's Math Arguments
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Betting Against the Threshold Theorem
lesson.summary: Gil Kalai, an Israeli mathematician, argues on probabilistic and combinatorial grounds that real physical noise may not satisfy the independence and locality assumptions built into the quantum threshold theorem, which would mean fault-tolerant error correction cannot actually outrun noise the way its supporters expect.
lesson.body:
The error correction overhead chapter explained the basic promise of fault-tolerant quantum computing: if the physical error rate per operation is below a certain threshold, and errors behave in a sufficiently local and independent way, a quantum threshold theorem guarantees you can suppress a logical qubit's error rate arbitrarily far, simply by adding more physical qubits and more layers of error correcting code. That theorem is mathematically solid. Gil Kalai, a mathematician at Hebrew University known for work in combinatorics and theoretical computer science, has spent roughly two decades publicly questioning not the theorem's logic but one load bearing assumption: whether real physical noise actually behaves the way the theorem needs it to.

The general shape of Kalai's argument is this. The threshold theorem's proof relies on noise that is, roughly, local and stochastically independent across the system, meaning errors on different qubits do not conspire with each other in ways tied to what the computation is doing. Kalai has argued, through models and conjectures developed and refined over years of writing and public debate, that noise in a real quantum system might instead be correlated in a way that scales with the complexity or entanglement of the state being maintained, so that as engineers build larger, more entangled quantum computers, the effective noise gets systematically worse in step with the computation itself, rather than behaving like the generic, computation independent noise the theorem assumes. If correct, adding more physical qubits would not straightforwardly buy the exponential error suppression the theorem promises, because building a more capable machine would itself be degrading the noise environment the theorem depends on.

This is not a claim Kalai has made quietly. He has argued it in extended public writing and in debate with prominent quantum information researchers, including, by his own account, a wagered bet with the MIT theorist Aram Harrow over the feasibility of building a working quantum computer. The exact terms matter less than what the wager signals: a live, specific, falsifiable disagreement between serious researchers, not vague doubt from outside the field.

The empirical picture remains genuinely unsettled. In recent years, experimental groups have reported logical qubits whose error rates decreased as more physical qubits were added to encode them, a result often described as operating below threshold, and supporters of the mainstream roadmap point to results like these as evidence against Kalai style correlated noise models. Kalai and researchers sympathetic to his concerns can reasonably respond that demonstrations at modest scale do not rule out correlated noise effects that only dominate at the much larger scales fault-tolerant algorithms will eventually require, so the disagreement has moved to what happens further up the scaling curve rather than being resolved.

It is worth being precise about what kind of skepticism this is, since it is easy to caricature. Kalai is not arguing quantum mechanics is wrong, nor that quantum computing is impossible by some law of physics. He is making a mathematical argument about which noise models are realistic, a question inside probability theory and mathematical physics rather than a rejection of quantum theory itself. That framing is why working quantum information theorists, even those who disagree with his conclusion, tend to treat his critique as a serious open question about modeling assumptions rather than fringe contrarianism.
